texts.159g-emuG-u1A:
This excerpt is interesting, because in 2023, after an extended period of internal review, they decided to dissolve their municipal governments ( the RZAMs and Juntas ) in favor of giving more power to the Local Autonomous Government of each community, coordinated by regional collectives which are subordinate to the Local Autonomous Governments, rather than superordinate.

In most institutions, as they get older they become more hierarchical. The Zapatistas did a review, and decided to de-hierarchize. Did they write a book on leadership? Nope. Did they set up a certification program? Nope. They just changed the system.

I should note, I am tempering my enthusiasm here for others to consider. The Zapatista form of autonomy emerges from Indigenous communities that share not only history, but language, family, and decades of struggle to defend their lands. It’s not something that can be imitated overnight by a new ecovillage, because most of the system is not visible.

Another thing the Zapatistas say is that Zapatismo is not something that can be imported or exported. It’s not a diagram to be copied, but rather a way of learning. If what they’re doing doesn’t work, they’ll change it.

However, it does not validate my view that communities should move towards an economy that does not have external money entering it, that all money in the community comes from a common purse, and that there is no money for internal necessities. The Zapatistas do use collective work to fund their communal functions like schools, clinics, autonomous government, resistance, etc., but they also bring in money through sales and trade, as well as support from outside. What the Zapatistas do validate is the idea that a community can choose to not purchase on the market most of its necessities, as well as it’s public functions, and instead rely on collective governance to fulfill those needs. They also show that while outside help can be useful for building capacity, outside specialists can also create new gatekeepers if the community becomes dependent on them.
texts.159g-emuG-u1B:
This is interesting, because in 2023 they went through a long process and decided to dissolve their level of municipal governance (Municipios Rebeldes Zapatistas and Juntas de Buen Gobierno) and move that to a more local level (Gobierno Local Autonomo), with more local/regional coordinating collectives, but making clear that those are subordinate to the different local governments.

The thing I find most interesting here, is that, in most institutions, as time goes on more and more layers and organs are added, but in their period of review, the EZLN took the opposite approach. And did they publish a book about how the proper exercise of leadership requires relinquishing power? Nope. Did they create a certification program for empowering leadership at all levels? Nope. They simply made the structural change that they needed.

Also, a note of caution here. This level of autonomy, while in theory applicable to many contexts, is born out of very strong communities with long histories (Indigenous communities that share language, family ties, long struggles for land, long periods of defending what they have, etc.) So it's not something a new ecovillage can just "copy" in terms of what is visible.

Additionally, the Zapatistas themselves say that Zapatismo cannot be imported or exported. What can be "imported" is the idea of building and asking questions, and when things don't work, changing the structure so that they will.

This, however, does not prove my point about moving to a model where internal necessities are not purchased, creating a common purse, and eventually eliminating the need for outside money altogether. The Zapatistas do use collective work for many things (schools, clinics, autonomous government, resistance activities, etc.), but also produce things for sale, engage in trade, and receive support from outside. However, what they do show is that it is possible for an entire community to eliminate the need to purchase, on the market, most major necessities and public functions. It may be helpful to bring in outside help to build capacities, but it's important to realize that if that help is indispensable, then the person/organization providing the help becomes a gatekeeper, and an asymmetric power dynamic of dependence is created.
texts.159g-emuG-u2A:
In the course of my research for this website, I looked for info about what ex-Escuelita students have done after they went home. I found lots of great stuff about alumni networking, what they have done to incorporate what they learned into their lives, and organizations they have started since being there, but nothing that connects a new organization directly to the Escuelita and then follows the fortunes of its members and their children. This is not to say that the Zapatistas are not influential outside Mexico, even before the Escuelita, only that influence does not necessarily have to be causal in order to be compelling. I am not proposing that the Zapatistas have shown the way to a successful model. I am, however, proposing a model for teaching that attempt to replicate that success.

Sociocracy has a very different history, yet many of the same features have emerged there as well: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority with linking between the levels of authority. Does this mean that there is a universal formula for making this work? No. But it means that people interested in building institutions of this sort have another place to look for things to learn.
texts.159g-emuG-u2B:
In the context of this research I have looked for evidence of the long-term impact of the Escuelita. While I found plenty of information of people networking, bringing practice back with them and organising, I couldn’t find evidence of the causal chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then setting up a communal institution and then good evidence about how well its members and their children have done. As I have also found evidence of Zapatista influence abroad before the Escuelita, it’s hard to prove that the Escuelita was responsible for some other institutions resembling Zapatista institutions. Nonetheless I’m trying their teaching method of “try this and see if it works for, if it does, try to replicate” rather than “first prove it works and then try to convince others”.

Sociocracy has a completely different history, yet they also ended up with circles, decision-making by consent, distributing authority and ways of connecting the levels. Does this prove that there is one universal formula for this? Of course not. But it gives people who want to build something similar a good system to study.
